section: Section Five — Rambam's Approach to the Commentary
subtitle: Rambam's methodology and a survey of the Tannaitic generations
author: Moses Maimonides
intro: Rambam's general introduction to his Commentary on the Mishnah — tracing the oral tradition from Sinai through the Zugot, Rebbi's compilation of the Mishnah, the Talmud and Geonim, and his own methodology. Original 12th-century Judeo-Arabic with English translation.

ג'מיע אלשארחין, והו אני את'בת כלאם אלמשנה
אלי אכ'ר אלהלכה, ת'ם אתכלם עלי תפסיר
תלך אלהלכה חסב מא צ'מנא, ת'ם אכ'ד' פי

כלאם.
aligned.en: I have judged it best that the arrangement of my work should follow what all commentators do: namely, that I set down the text of the mishnah through to the end of the *halakhah*, and then discuss the explanation of that *halakhah* in accordance with what it contains; then I take up a second *halakhah*, and so on to the end of the Mishnah. Every *halakhah* that is self-evident I shall simply write out without offering any comment upon it.

אלסתם מדפוע ואינה הלכה. ואמא סאיר
אלאכ'תלאפאת פלא נלג'יך פיהא אלי פכרה,
בל אקול לך אלהלכה עלי מד'הב מן הי, ולו
כאן יחיד ורבים אקול הלכה כחכמים.
aligned.en: Likewise, every *setam* mishnah—one in which there is no dispute—is to be acted upon as it states the matter, except in anomalous cases; and in those anomalous *halakhot* I shall tell you that this *setam* is overridden and is not the [accepted] law. As for the remaining disputes, I shall not compel you to any reflection of your own, but shall tell you whose view the law follows; and even where the dispute is between an individual and the majority, I shall say "the law is according to the Sages."
